source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Founding statement of MADIL. A program is a pair of models: an input model that decomposes the input grid into parts, and an output model that builds the output from those parts. Learning picks the pair of models that compresses the examples most, by two-part MDL, L(M,E)=L(M)+L(E|M).
numbers: Search is narrow and deep, not wide and shallow. One CPU thread, 180s budget per task. Score 7% at ArcPrize 2024 private, up from 2% at ARCathon 2022.
quote: The model that best describes the data is the one that compresses it the most
limits: Hand-built DSL of core-knowledge primitives. Stays well below LLM scores.
agent_relevance: S2 and S7: a concrete template for a description language and a compression score used as the search signal, with code (not a model) choosing.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Description lengths are Shannon code lengths, L(v|V) = -log2 f_V(v), from explicit value distributions. Task model length = L(input model) + L(output model given input variables).
numbers: Value types: sprites, masks, vectors, objects, colors, motifs. Background color: black more likely; object color: black less likely.
limits: Priors are hand-set. The answer depends on how well these code lengths match real task regularities.
agent_relevance: A usable simplicity score needs a defined coding scheme. An agent that says 'simplest' without one has no measure.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: The data term is up-weighted by a rehearsal factor (default 100) because the 3.3 training pairs stand in for many valid pairs. Too low stops search early. Too high favours overfitting. A normalised DL gives inputs and outputs equal weight.
numbers: Rehearsal factor 100 for ARC in 2025; 10 in the 2021 paper. Normalised DL lies in [0,2].
limits: The factor is tuned by hand on the training set.
agent_relevance: Model cost versus data fit is a real knob. For our G3 rule: fitting the given examples is cheap, so weigh complexity explicitly.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Public evaluation set (400 tasks, never looked at during design): MADIL finds a model correct on all train examples for 69 tasks. 57 are correct on all test examples, a generalisation rate of 82%. Two more tasks gave correct predictions from a model right on 1 of 2 train examples.
numbers: 69 fit, 57 correct, 12 fit-but-wrong (about 18%). 53 of 57 correct on the first attempt. Micro-accuracy used.
limits: Evaluation set was not used for design, so this is a clean test. Absolute level is low (about 14%).
agent_relevance: Direct measure of the wrong-but-fitting rate under MDL: about 1 in 6 fitted programs fails at test. Matches our own G3 finding.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Table 6 comparison. MADIL v3.5: 32.1% on training tasks, about 15.1% on public evaluation, 7.0% on the private set. Icecuber (Kaggle 2020): about 44.7% train, 30.8% eval, 20.6% private. M. Hodel (ARCathon 2022): 6.0% private. MindsAI 55.5% and The Architects 53.5% private (ArcPrize 2024).
numbers: The column layout in the extracted table is garbled. Train 32.1 and private 7.0 for MADIL are clear. Eval 15.1 is inferred and agrees with 57 to 69 of 400 tasks.
limits: Private figures for proprietary-LLM systems are n/a because they need internet.
agent_relevance: Program search by MDL alone is far behind brute-force DSL search (Icecuber) and LLM systems on ARC-1.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Model sizes. For the 57 correct solutions the model size (count of values, references, functions, patterns, unknowns) ranges 3 to 46, mean 15.2. Only 4 tasks have a correct solution of size 4 or less.
numbers: Brute-force DSL search is limited to depth 3-4 in prior work. A mean depth of 15 would be intractable without a guiding score.
limits: Size counts are in MADIL's own primitive set, not comparable to other DSLs.
agent_relevance: Description length works as a search guide that reaches depth 15 where blind search stops at 3-4. Supports using a length score to prune.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Search efficiency. Of 69 solved tasks, 54 solutions are found on the very first MCTS rollout (plain greedy compression). Average rank of the best model is 1.3 for solved tasks (1.6 over all 400). 80% of solutions appear within 20s of a 180s budget.
numbers: Mean models visited: 177 (all 400 tasks), 45 (the 69 solved). Mean depth 17 (all) and 11 (solved). Deepest 43.
quote: Strikingly, 80% solutions are found in the first 20s
limits: MCTS adds a few tasks over greedy; the ablation shows it recovers from local minima (3-4 tasks lost without).
agent_relevance: When MDL is the signal, early greedy steps usually suffice. Extra search buys a few tasks. Fits G1: search more only when stuck.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Ablation on 71 evaluation tasks solved by some MADIL v3.2-3.6 version. One sampled description (Np=1) loses 19 tasks; one top description (Kp=1) loses 6. Np=10 vs 100 or Kp=2 vs 3 lose 1 task. Search-related cuts lose 3-4 tasks. Expression cap Se=5 vs 9: no loss.
numbers: Only decreases of each parameter were tested, one at a time, on a 71-task sample.
limits: Robust overall: strong effects only at Np=1 and Se=1. The sample is tasks already solved, so it cannot show what helps unsolved tasks.
agent_relevance: Keeping several candidate descriptions of each example matters most. Echoes keeping multiple readings alive before committing.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Overlap with brute force. On public evaluation tasks MADIL is fully correct on 59 and Icecuber on 117 (twice as many). 43 are shared and 16 are solved only by MADIL.
numbers: Strict count: all test outputs must be right. Icecuber rerun by the author from open source.
limits: Complementary, not dominated: 16 of 59 are unique to MDL.
agent_relevance: A program-search tool and a compression tool solve different tasks. Use both rather than one.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Failure analysis on training tasks. 21 tasks: model found but wrong on test; the main cause is spurious expressions that patch over a wrong decomposition, and risk rises with fewer examples and larger allowed expressions. 62 tasks: solvable in principle but not found; 21 need a non-compressive step first, 15 lack diverse top descriptions, 13 other causes.
numbers: Counts are on the 400 training tasks.
limits: The author suggests late-acceptance hill-climbing to allow non-compressive steps, and a revised code length for expressions.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for our G3: examples-only MDL fit can be spurious. Also: greedy compression can need a temporary loss, so do not block all uphill moves.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Pruning step. After search, constants and patterns in the input model are replaced by unknowns whenever accuracy does not drop. Example: task 47c1f68c, the black background becomes an unknown. Test inputs are also parse-checked against the input model.
numbers: Not applied to the output model, since it would add predicted outputs and cut accuracy.
limits: Widens the rule's domain but can still overfit unseen cases.
agent_relevance: A cheap, code-run generalisation step: drop every detail the answer does not need. Candidate for an S7 check.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: Stated limits. No conditionals or recursion. Parsing one grid at a time, so no cross-example consistency. Input and output models learned separately. No n-ary expressions (combinatorial blow-up). Missing primitives (staircases, symmetry completion, object similarity).
numbers: Author says adding primitives alone is unlikely to solve ARC and may give ad-hoc solutions.
limits: Honest list; none of it is measured in a full ablation.
agent_relevance: Marks where a pure compression approach stops. Do not expect MDL alone to cover conditional or multi-example rules.

source: Ferre (2025) MADIL: An MDL-based Framework for Efficient Program Synthesis in the ARC Benchmark
finding: MCTS design. States are task models, actions are transitions, value = 1 - 0.5 * normalised DL, UCB1 with c=2, rollout is greedy to the end, stop when a correct model is found or time runs out. Pure decomposition patterns are not compressive, so they are tried by an extended lookahead.
numbers: Table 3 defaults: Np=100, Kp=3, Ng=Kg=3, Se=6, Ne=1000, Kt=100, K=3 attempts (2 at ArcPrize).
limits: Design is reported; only greedy is compared against it.
agent_relevance: A ready recipe: compression gain as the reward, greedy with restarts.

source: Ferre (2021) First Steps of an Approach to the ARC Challenge based on Descriptive Grid Models and MDL
finding: Early version (descriptive grid models plus MDL). On the 400 training tasks, solved tasks rose from 5 to 29 over one year with a 30s limit per task, only by improving models and search. Evaluation tasks: 6 of 400 (1.5%).
numbers: 29/400 (7.25%) train and 6/400 (1.5%) eval at v2.2, 30s timeout.
limits: Evaluation results were far below training; the author deliberately did not look at evaluation tasks.
agent_relevance: Shows the slow, manual path of improving a primitive set. Each version needed human design.

source: Ferre (2021) First Steps of an Approach to the ARC Challenge based on Descriptive Grid Models and MDL
finding: Version table. v1.0 (Oct 2020) train 8 fit / 5 test-correct. v2.0 at 120s: 35 fit / 24 correct. v2.1 at 120s: 38 / 28. v2.2 at 30s: 41 fit, 29 test-correct on train; on eval 8 fit, 6 correct.
numbers: Counts are fit-on-train vs correct-on-test. The gap is 7 to 12 tasks in later versions.
limits: The fit-but-wrong gap persists across versions.
agent_relevance: First hard numbers on how often a compressive fit fails at test: 12 of 41 on train at v2.2.

source: Ferre (2021) First Steps of an Approach to the ARC Challenge based on Descriptive Grid Models and MDL
finding: Causes of fit-but-wrong in 11 training tasks: wrong constant-versus-variable choice and accidental arithmetic equalities (0962bcdd); wrong segmentation, preferring a full rectangle (1caeab9d); the transform should repeat more times in test (29c11459); invariance to rotation or transposition (4522001f).
numbers: 11 tasks listed at 60s, v2.0.
limits: Four concrete failure types.
agent_relevance: A checklist for G3 checks: accidental equalities, segmentation, repeat count, orientation invariance.

source: Ferre (2021) First Steps of an Approach to the ARC Challenge based on Descriptive Grid Models and MDL
finding: Two-part MDL with the data term multiplied by 10 (each example counts 10) to allow more complex models, since ARC has about 3 examples per task. A bitmap costs height times width bits. Background color has a strong prior toward black.
numbers: Factor 10 in 2021; 100 in 2025.
limits: The weight was chosen by hand.
agent_relevance: The weight moved by 10x between versions, so it is a design choice, not a constant of nature.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: CompressARC. A 76K-parameter network with no pretraining, trained at inference time on only the target puzzle (test output hidden) by minimising a variational estimate of description length: reconstruction error plus the KL cost of a latent code. Framed as code-golf: the shortest self-contained program that prints the dataset with solutions filled in.
numbers: 20% of 400 evaluation puzzles and 34.75% of 400 training puzzles at pass@2 after 2000 steps, about 20 minutes per puzzle (RTX 4070).
limits: Weights are counted in bits, which turns program search into gradient descent.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that an MDL objective alone gives correct generalisation on ARC with no external data.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: Baselines on the ARC-AGI-1 evaluation sets at pass@2: random guess 0%; brute-force rule search 40% (cited private figure); U-Net trained only on the demo pairs 0.75%; CompressARC 20%; HRM ablation 31%; HRM 40.3%; OpenAI o3 high 87.5% (semi-private).
numbers: The paper's own U-Net control gets 0.75% under the same data limits, so MDL and not just test-time training drives the gain.
limits: Datasets differ per row (private, public eval, semi-private), so not strictly comparable.
agent_relevance: MDL objective vs plain test-time fitting on the same data: 20% vs 0.75%. Compression, not mere fitting, matters.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: Accuracy rises with inference steps and with allowed guesses. Training set pass@2 goes 2.25% at 100 steps to 34.75% at 2000. Pass@1 1% to 30.25%; pass@10 41.5%; pass@1000 52.75%. Evaluation pass@2 reaches 20.0% at the last point.
numbers: Eval pass@2 by steps (100 to 2000): 1.25, 6, 10.75, 13.75, 15, 17.75, 19.25, 20.75, 21.5, 20.0 percent. The last point is below the 1500-step value.
limits: The full training set takes 130 hours of GPU time at 2000 steps.
agent_relevance: More compute turns into accuracy smoothly. Pass@k with a good selector would add a lot. Shows both a ceiling and a compute cost.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: Observed abilities and disabilities. It can infill, crop, connect dots with lines including diagonals, detect same color and adjacency, and detect connectivity. It fails at long-range pattern extension (puzzle 28e73c20): it extends a short distance and then guesses.
numbers: Abilities were listed from watching runs, with no controlled test.
limits: Limits come from the network layers, not from MDL itself.
agent_relevance: Gives a profile of what compression-only learning cannot do: long-range structure.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: Case study Color the Boxes (puzzle 272f95fa). After training, the latent code holds a color-to-direction table and row and column divider positions. The top principal component of the direction table is 829 times stronger than the next.
numbers: One hand-picked puzzle.
limits: Interpretation by the authors from the weights.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the shortest code recovers the same rule a human states.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning (BARC)
finding: Induction (a neural model writes a Python program) and transduction (a neural model predicts the output grid) solve different ARC tasks even when trained on the same synthetic data. The sets they solve are stable across random restarts, so the split is not noise.
numbers: Validation accuracy, 2 tries: ARC-Heavy induction 30.5%; transduction with TTT 43.25%. ARC-Potpourri induction 38.0%; transduction with TTT 43.0%.
quote: Inductive program synthesis excels at precise computations, and at composing multiple concepts
limits: Contradicts the RobustFill finding that induction was superior. Here neither dominates.
agent_relevance: Program output and direct answers are complementary. An ensemble beats either, so keep both a program path and a direct path.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning (BARC)
finding: Ensemble of induction and transduction reaches 56.75% on ARC validation (2 tries), against average human 60.2% and best human 97.8%. Akyurek et al. later reached 61.9% using BARC's synthesizer.
numbers: Top numbers need 10k to 20k sampled programs per task. A scaled-down version scored 19% on Kaggle private and 36.5% on validation.
quote: Our best model performs nearly as well as the average human (56.75% vs. 60.2%)
limits: Scaled down because the flagship model was too expensive for the Kaggle private set.
agent_relevance: Program sampling with an execution check scales with sample count. This is code-selected, as in our G5.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning (BARC)
finding: Difficulty versus humans. Models beat humans on the hardest 20% of validation problems and trail them on the easiest. Authors read this as: some problems are simple in code but hard for people, and people have priors the program generator lacks.
numbers: Five difficulty classes built from human data (LeGris et al. 2024).
limits: Observed pattern, no causal test.
agent_relevance: Code-length difficulty and human difficulty differ. The shortest program is not what humans find easy.

source: Akyurek et al. (2024) The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning
finding: Test-time training of an 8B language model on augmented in-context examples reaches 53.0% on the ARC public validation set, up to 6x a fine-tuned baseline. Combined with BARC's program synthesizer: 58.5% to 62.8%, headline 61.9%.
numbers: TTT on the BARC model 53.0%; own fine-tuned model 47.1%; semi-private evaluation 47.5%, a decline from validation.
limits: Authors suggest the semi-private drop may reflect a harder distribution.
agent_relevance: Program synthesis still adds several points on top of strong TTT. Combine, do not replace.

source: Akyurek et al. (2024) The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning
finding: With the TTT pipeline, BARC's neural model solves 73.5% of the tasks that BARC's program-synthesis model solves, up from 42.2% without TTT.
numbers: Overlap measured on ARC validation.
limits: Single lab, from the discussion section.
agent_relevance: Test-time adaptation closes much of the gap to program solutions, so a program path is partly replaceable.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models
finding: GPT-4 hypothesis search on a random 100-task ARC subset. Direct answer 17%. Program only 23%. Summarised hypotheses (64 proposed, 8 kept, 8 programs each, 3 execution-feedback rounds) 30%. Human-selected hypotheses 33%. Icecuber answers 43% of the same 100.
numbers: GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 tasks. Of those, 33 (67%) gave correct programs with human selection. Top-1 scoring. Chain-of-thought without programs: 19%.
quote: if a working program was found, it almost always generalized
limits: The authors warn other tasks may need work against false positives.
agent_relevance: LLM program synthesis checked by running on examples beat plain prompting by 13 points. Its low false-positive claim differs from MADIL's 18% and rests on a small sample.

source: Chollet et al. (2026) ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
finding: History in the ARC-AGI-2 paper. The 2020 Kaggle winner scored 20% private, but the union of tasks solved by any team was 49%, mostly via brute-force program search. The authors call this a weakness and design ARC-AGI-2 to be less brute-forcible.
numbers: ArcPrize 2024: MindsAI 55.5% (ineligible), The Architects 53.5%. o3 preview 76% low-compute (about 200 dollars per task) and 88% high-compute (about 20,000 dollars per task) on semi-private ARC-AGI-1.
limits: Costs are estimates by the benchmark owners.
agent_relevance: Bound on what program search shows: nearly half of ARC-1 private tasks are brute-force reachable.

source: Chollet et al. (2026) ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
finding: ARC-AGI-2 human testing: 407 participants, 515 sessions, 1,848 task-test pairs, 13,405 attempts, 62% successful. Every task in the public eval, semi-private and private sets was solved by at least two independent humans. Frontier-model scores on the new set are low.
numbers: Scores below 5% are treated as noise by the owners.
quote: ARC-AGI-2 accuracies below 5% are generally not treated as meaningful
limits: Scores are measured by the benchmark owners.
agent_relevance: Brute-force and compression approaches both fall on ARC-AGI-2 by design. MDL results on ARC-1 should not be read as general.

source: Chollet (2019) On the Measure of Intelligence
finding: Chollet defines generalisation difficulty using algorithmic complexity: the length of the shortest program that outputs a string on a fixed universal machine. A task's generalisation difficulty is the fraction of its shortest solution not explained by the shortest optimal training-time solution.
numbers: Defined formally, no numbers.
limits: Kolmogorov complexity is not computable, so it is a conceptual yardstick, not a score.
agent_relevance: The ARC authors frame skill as short-program discovery, giving the MDL line its theory base.

source: Grunwald (2004) A tutorial introduction to the minimum description length principle
finding: MDL tutorial. Crude two-part MDL picks the hypothesis H that minimises L(H) + L(D|H), in bits. Refined MDL replaces two-part codes with universal codes (NML), which avoid arbitrariness in how H is encoded.
numbers: Sections on crude MDL, two-part codes as simple universal codes, and NML as an optimal universal model.
limits: MADIL and the 2021 paper use crude two-part MDL, so they inherit dependence on hand-chosen codes.
agent_relevance: Explains why MADIL's hand-set priors and rehearsal weight matter: crude MDL is only as good as its code.

source: Ellis et al. (2020/2023) DreamCoder
finding: DreamCoder wake-sleep. Wake searches for programs with high posterior (likelihood times a prior favouring short description length). Sleep grows a library of abstractions chosen to compress solved programs, under an MDL/Bayes objective.
numbers: Program learner; ARC is not its main benchmark.
limits: Learns primitives from tasks, which MADIL's author names as an open research problem.
agent_relevance: A source for learning a subgoal library by compression, relevant to our subgoal vocabulary.

source: Hodel (2024) Addressing the ARC via Procedural Example Generation (re-arc)
finding: re-arc. Hodel built a generator for each ARC training task so any number of new examples can be sampled, widening the example space where the originals are narrow.
numbers: Dataset note. Accuracy results were not in the text read.
limits: Only the opening motivation was read in detail.
agent_relevance: A source of extra examples for held-out checks (G3) when the given examples are few.
